stem.text: The government of a country allows each factory in the fertiliser industry to discharge 10 000 litres of liquid waste into the rivers each year.
If a factory discharges less than 10 000 litres, it can sell its remaining allowance to another factory that wants to discharge more than 10 000 litres.

explanation.text: A pollution (or tradeable) permit gives a firm the legal right to pollute up to a set limit, and critically allows firms with spare allowance to sell it to firms that need more — creating a market price for the right to pollute and an incentive for low-polluting firms to cut emissions further (to sell their unused allowance) while high-polluting firms pay for the privilege.

optionAnalysis.text: An embargo is a ban on trade or an activity altogether — the scenario explicitly allows discharge up to a limit and lets firms trade their allowance, not a total ban.
A tradeable pollution permit is exactly a set discharge allowance that can be bought and sold between firms, matching the scenario described.
A tariff is a tax on imported goods, unrelated to a domestic discharge allowance scheme.
A subsidy is a payment from government to encourage an activity (e.g. to reduce pollution), not an allowance that firms trade among themselves.

reasoningChain: Identify the key features described: a capped discharge amount (10,000 litres) per factory, and the ability to sell unused allowance to another factory.
Match these features to the definition of a tradeable pollution permit: a government-set, tradeable right to pollute up to a limit.
Rule out embargo (a ban), tariff (an import tax) and subsidy (a government payment), none of which involve a tradeable allowance.

inferredMistakes.text: Associating any government pollution-control policy with a tax or subsidy by default, missing the distinguishing tradeable feature that identifies this specifically as a permit scheme.
